diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since the $\ell_i$ ($i>0$) are all independent, it follows that

issues.failure_explanation: The induction step infers that $\ell_{n+1}=\ell(c_n,r_n)$ is independent of the whole vector $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ from the hypothesis that $r_n$ is independent of each $\ell_i$ separately. Marginal independence of $r_n$ from every $\ell_i$ does not imply independence from the joint vector (pairwise does not imply mutual independence), and propagating the hypothesis to the next step (e.g. that $r_{n+1}$ is independent of the earlier $\ell_i$) requires the same missing joint argument. The needed fact — $c_n$ is independent of the entire history $\sigma(r_0,c_0,\dots,c_{n-1})$, and if $r_n$ is jointly independent of $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ then the pair $(c_n,r_n)$, hence $(\ell_{n+1},r_{n+1})$, is independent of that vector — is never stated or proved. Corollary cor:added-2 then computes $\mathbb{E}[\prod_{i\le n}\ell_i]=\prod_{i\le n}\mathbb{E}[\ell_i]$, which requires mutual independence, not the pairwise statement (ii).

failure_location.quote: Assume that $r_n$ is independent from $\ell_i$ ($i=1,\dots,n$). The base case is validated by the computations above. $\ell_{n+1}$ depends only upon $r_n$ and $c_n$ in its construction. $c_n$ is clearly independent from all $\ell_i$. By the induction hypothesis, we can say the same about $r_n$. Thus, $\ell_{n+1}$ is independent from $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ for all $n>0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the induction hypothesis to joint independence of $r_n$ from $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$, note that $c_n$ is independent of $(r_n,\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ since it is independent of the whole history, and apply the one-step computation of part (i) to conclude $(\ell_{n+1},r_{n+1})\perp(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$; this proves (ii) in mutual form and propagates the strengthened hypothesis.
issues.overall_effect: The proofs of Theorem thm - ind (ii) and of the product formula $\mathbb{E}[L_n]=\mathbb{E}[\ell_1]^n$ in cor:added-2 are incomplete as written; the statements themselves are correct.
issues.title: Independence induction conflates marginal with joint independence
issues.why_classification: The missing step is a short, standard conditional-independence observation inserted locally in the same proof; no statement, rate, or guarantee changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\mathcal{T}: X \to Y$ be a positive linear operator preserving linear functions.
Since $\mathcal{T}(G_n)$ is a cumulative density function, it is clearly positive and bounded.
The iterated \emph{Dyadic map} ($c=1/2$) is a well-known chaotic dynamical system
let us note that the conditions in \Cref{thm - root_conv} are optimal

issues.failure_explanation: The proof applies the Gavrea–Ivan theorem (thm - conv), which requires $\mathcal{T}$ to be a positive linear operator on $B_\circ[0,1]$. Positivity is only checked for nondecreasing CDF inputs; in fact $\mathcal{T}$ is not positive on $B_\circ[0,1]$: for cuts $c\equiv 0.35$ (allowed by the hypotheses) and the nonnegative function $G=\mathbf{1}_{[0.3,0.35]}\in B_\circ[0,1]$, $(\mathcal{T}G)(0.05)=G(0.0175)+G(0.3825)-G(0.35)=-1<0$. So the cited theorem is used outside its hypotheses. Worse, the stated conclusion is false within the stated regime: with deterministic midpoint cuts $c_n\equiv 1/2$ (allowed — they are not a.s. at 0 or 1 — and explicitly included in the paper's family as the classical bisection) and deterministic initial root $r_0\equiv 1/3$ (no point mass at 0 or 1; fixed roots are even used in the paper's own simulations), $T(1/2,\cdot)$ is the doubling map and the orbit $1/3\mapsto 2/3\mapsto 1/3$ is periodic, so $\mathcal{T}^kG_0$ alternates between the CDFs of point masses at $1/3$ and $2/3$ and never converges to $t$; the sup-norm distance stays at $2/3$, also violating the advertised rate bound. Any atomic initial root under dyadic cuts keeps an atomic law forever, so the claim fails for the discrete cut/root distributions the paper's Lebesgue–Stieltjes framework explicitly advertises, and the subsequent assertion that the stated conditions are 'optimal' is also incorrect.

failure_location.quote: If $r_0$ does not have a point mass at $0$ or $1$ (that is, $\mathbb{P}[r_0=0]=\mathbb{P}[r_0=1]=0$) and if the cuts $c_n$ are not almost surely at 0 or 1, then

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must exclude the atomic/deterministic regimes (e.g. require the cut distribution to be absolutely continuous or otherwise mixing, and/or restrict the initial law) and supply a genuinely new convergence proof, because the operator is not positive on $B_\circ[0,1]$, so Theorem thm - conv cannot be applied to it under any hypotheses consistent with the counterexample.
issues.overall_effect: The central convergence claim of Section 3 — repeated in the abstract, introduction and conclusion — that $\mathcal{T}^kG_0\to t$ uniformly with rate $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ for any initial root distribution without endpoint atoms and any cut distribution not degenerate at $\{0,1\}$, is unproved and false as stated. The convergence parts of thm - pdf_general and cor - mean_variance_gen and the rate estimates in the closing remark of Section 3 all rest on it; the claimed optimality of the hypotheses fails; the numerical 'validation' of the rate in Section 5 concerns the same claim.
issues.title: Convergence to the uniform law for arbitrary initial distributions is false as stated; the cited iterate theorem is applied without its positivity hypothesis
issues.why_classification: A central theorem is false in an explicitly advertised regime (discrete and even deterministic cuts are covered by the paper's framework, and the classical bisection $c\equiv1/2$ is a showcased special case), and its only proof relies on a cited theorem applied outside its hypotheses. Every supported resolution either abandons the 'arbitrary distributions' scope — a central quantifier of the paper — or requires essentially new convergence machinery, and the downstream convergence results and rate guarantees fall with it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The initial root distribution is always $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, so $\mu_{\ell_n}\to 2/3$.
By contrast, the asymmetric distributions converge more slowly, at a rate closer to the upper bound given by the theorem.

issues.failure_explanation: The protocol states the cuts are drawn from $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, under which the theoretical decay rate $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ of Theorem thm - root_conv equals $2/3$ for every initial distribution. Instead, the 'Theoretical' row of Table tab:convrate lists $0.6, 0.7714\dots, 0.9385\dots, 0.508\overline{3}$, which are exactly the values of $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ for cuts drawn from $\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)$, $\mathrm{Beta}(0.5,2)$, $\mathrm{Beta}(0.1,2)$ and $\mathrm{Bates}(20)$ respectively (the same numbers as in Table tab:scalingfactors), and the discussion compares the fitted rates to those per-column bounds. Conversely, the sentence 'The initial root distribution is always $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, so $\mu_{\ell_n}\to 2/3$' contradicts both the stated protocol (initial roots are drawn from $\mathcal{R}$) and the per-column limits. Under genuinely uniform cuts, the fitted rates $0.736$ and $0.914$ would even exceed the $2/3$ theoretical bound, contradicting the theorem the experiment is meant to validate. The source therefore does not determine which experiment was actually performed.
